paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 1.  English translation of source: “‘Our teachers taught: For three transgressions women die at the time of childbirth. All three have their basis in the Torah: niddah, as it is written, ‘If a woman has a flow [of blood]’; challah, ‘The first of your dough’; and the lighting of a lamp, as it is written, ‘You shall call Shabbos a delight’—this refers to kindling the Shabbos lamp. If you should say that one might sit in darkness, that is not delight, for those who descend to Gehinnom are judged in darkness, as it says, ‘A land of deepest gloom, like darkness.’’ The Midrash continues: ‘Why were women commanded concerning these three mitzvos? ... She caused [Adam] to die and shed his blood ... She defiled the challah of the world ... She extinguished Adam’s lamp, as it is written, ‘The soul of man is the lamp of the Lord’; therefore she must attend to kindling the lamp.’”  Context and connection: The source develops both sides of Rav Tzadok’s argument: the three practices address the loss introduced by the first sin, while light is the positive image of Shabbos restoration. The relevant lamp passage occurs in Noach 1 in the commonly indexed Sefaria edition; Rav Tzadok's printed numbering differs.

Further parallel — Tzidkat HaTzadik 13 [paragraph 1] (English translation as supplied in Akiva Publishing interlinear library):  “Time is composed of day and night, and so too is human life: light and darkness, ascending and descending, as is known from the Baal Shem Tov's teaching on the verse: "Seven times does the righteous fall and rise up" (Proverbs 24:16). For seven days constitute one week, and thereafter those same seven days recur in cycle. Indeed, even during the period of darkness one needs the light of the moon or the stars, which is also recognized as light (Pesachim 2a), so that it not be total obscurity. And inside one's house, one requires the light of a candle”

Connection to this note: Rav Tzadok elsewhere explicitly places the mitzvah-candle within the inner experience of human darkness. This adds a second passage on the candle motif beyond the Tanchuma cited in the note.

paragraphs.text: Job 10:21–22.  English translation of source: “‘Before I depart—and do not return—to the land of darkness and the shadow of death: a land of thick gloom, like utter darkness; of deathly shadow and disorder, where even its radiance is like darkness.’”  Context and connection: The surrounding verse describes the realm of death, not the laws of Shabbos. Tanchuma borrows this vivid image for Gehinnom. Rav Tzadok then treats the light of a Shabbos lamp as more than physical convenience: it represents an opposite spiritual condition, one of order, comfort and revealed divine presence.

Further parallel — Tzidkat HaTzadik 261 [paragraph 1] (English translation as supplied in Akiva Publishing interlinear library):  “The Holy One, blessed be He, His glory fills the whole earth, and there is no place devoid of Him, only that He is in deep concealment, "He made darkness His secret place" (Psalms 18:12). And when this recognition shines into man's heart—how Hashem fills the whole earth with His glory— this is termed "He brought us forth from darkness to a great light," as recited in the Haggadah.”

Connection to this note: This explains why darkness is not simply absence of physical illumination: it can signify the concealment of a divine reality that becomes perceptible when recognition awakens.

English translation of the Hebrew: “The righteous transform darkness into light. Connection to this footnote: Darkness becomes the starting point of spiritual illumination, rather than merely an image of punishment.

paragraphs.text: Genesis 1:2; Midrash Tanchuma, Bo 2.  English translation of source: “Genesis 1:2: ‘The earth was unformed and empty, darkness was over the face of the deep, and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters.’ Midrash Tanchuma, Bo 2: ‘Rabbi Nechemiah said: [The darkness of Egypt came] from the darkness of Gehinnom, for it is said, ‘A land of thick gloom, like darkness, of deathly shadow and no order.’ ... With what are the wicked covered in Gehinnom? With darkness. Just as an earthenware jar is covered with an earthenware lid, so these wicked ones, whose deeds are in the dark, are covered by the Holy One, blessed be He, with the deep, which is darkness, as it says: ‘And darkness was upon the face of the deep.’ This is Gehinnom.’”  Context and connection: In the verse, darkness precedes creation’s illumination. In the Midrash it becomes a moral image: a person concealed in wrongdoing encounters concealment. Rav Tzadok juxtaposes this with the contrary possibility that divine judgment may awaken recognition and thereby itself be experienced as light.

Further parallel — Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvot, segment 1 [paragraph 13] (English translation as supplied in Akiva Publishing interlinear library):  “By day one gives precedence to light: "He forms light and creates darkness"; while at night one reverses it: "He rolls away light before darkness and darkness before light": for each blessing emphasizes the dominant quality of its own hour; and relative to the night, cessation and darkness take precedence over the light of day, matching the physical Creation of the cosmos: first came darkness and then came light (Shabbat 77b); for one who stands in darkness encounters darkness first, followed by the light.”

Connection to this note: The parallel passage identifies darkness-then-light as a recurring structure of Creation and spiritual perception, clarifying why the Midrash reads the primordial darkness as morally significant.

Connection to this footnote: The passage makes the transition from darkness to light essential to the recognition of divine goodness.

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 54a.  English translation of source: “‘This is no difficulty: one statement concerns our fire and one concerns the fire of Gehinnom. Our fire [was created] at the close of Shabbos; the fire of Gehinnom, on the eve of Shabbos. But was the fire of Gehinnom created on the eve of Shabbos? Was it not taught that seven things were created before the world: the Torah, repentance, the Garden of Eden, Gehinnom, the Throne of Glory, the Sanctuary, and the name of the Messiah? ... Rabbi Yose says: The fire created by the Holy One, blessed be He, on the second day never goes out, as it says, ‘Their fire shall not be quenched.’ ... Why was ‘for it was good’ not said on the second day? Because the fire of Gehinnom was created then.’”  Context and connection: Rav Tzadok deliberately focuses on the expression ‘the light of Gehinnom.’ He is not denying its punitive aspect. He argues that for one who accepts the truth of the judgment, the confrontation can illuminate what was previously hidden. The paradox depends on distinguishing revelatory light from the comfort of an ordinary flame.

Further parallel — Resisei Layla 48 [paragraph 7] (English translation as supplied in Akiva Publishing interlinear library):  “Our Sages of blessed memory also taught (Nedarim 8b) that in the future there will be no Gehinnom; rather, the sun will be removed from its sheath—the righteous, etc., and the wicked, etc. This follows the principle: 'The righteous shall walk in them, while sinners shall stumble in them.' Likewise, they taught (Shabbat 88b) that for those who turn to the left in Torah it becomes a potion of death; 'evil pursues sinners,' for the sin itself becomes the punishment.”

Connection to this note: Rav Tzadok elsewhere explicitly contrasts what one and the same revelation does to the righteous and to the wicked, illuminating the apparent paradox of Gehinnom being called light.

Connection to this footnote: This parallels Rav Tzadok’s reversal of Gehinnom imagery: a destructive fire can be countered by the inner fire of avodas Hashem.

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 19a; Isaiah 66:24.  English translation of source: “‘But did Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish not say: The wicked do not return in repentance even at the entrance to Gehinnom, as it is said, ‘They shall go out and look upon the corpses of the men who rebel against Me’ [Isaiah 66:24]? It does not say ‘who rebelled’ but ‘who rebel’—they go on rebelling forever! There is no difficulty: this statement concerns the sinners of Israel, and that statement the sinners of the nations of the world.’”  Context and connection: The distinction concerns how suffering is received, not merely whether punishment is severe. Rav Tzadok uses the sugya to explain that for a person who refuses teshuvah, judgment remains darkness because it produces no renewed recognition of Hashem.

Further parallel — Tzidkat HaTzadik 75 [paragraph 2] (English translation as supplied in Akiva Publishing interlinear library):  “Transgressions within the soul of an Israelite are not an essential acquisition, but merely incidental, and therefore they are subject to redemption, as it is stated: 'And He shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities' (Psalms 130:8).”

Connection to this note: The possibility of redeeming sin rather than treating it as an unchangeable identity helps explain the contrast between entrenched rebellion and genuine acceptance of divine judgment.

English translation of source: “Song of Songs 8:13: ‘You who dwell in the gardens, the companions listen for your voice; let me hear it.’ Shir HaShirim Rabbah, on this verse: ‘Rabbi Yirmeyah said in the name of Rabbi Chiyya the Great: Two companions who engage with one another in a matter of halachah and yield to one another in the argument—of them Scripture says, ‘Then those who fear the Lord spoke with one another, and the Lord paid attention and heard’ [Malachi 3:16]. ... paragraphs.text: Further parallel — Tiferet Yosef, Bereshit 2, paragraphs 5, 7, 9 (English translation as supplied in Akiva Publishing interlinear library):  ““A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day: It is good to give thanks to Hashem” (Psalms 92:1-2). My revered grandfather, my master and teacher, of blessed memory, explained regarding this that the ultimate purpose of the creation of heaven and earth is the Sabbath day. Meaning, during the six workdays, man acts and toils, and it appears to him that he himself is piercing the concealment and recognizing the revelation of the Kingdom of Heaven in the world. And afterwards, on the Sabbath day, man realizes: “What was the world lacking? Rest; the Sabbath came, rest came” (Rashi on Genesis 2:2) — meaning, he recognizes that even the very strength to toil was entirely granted by Hashem, and he recognizes that in truth, from the perspective of Hashem, all is without limit and without boundary; and that these boundaries which Hashem instituted were solely because He desired to bestow good upon His creations, wishing that the Jew should coronate Hashem through free choice, actively choosing the good and despising the bad. For had the revelation of the Kingdom of Heaven been completely explicit, there would be no free will whatsoever, as all would clearly recognize that it is impossible to flee from the Source of Life; therefore Hashem established these limitations.”

Connection to this note: The Ishbitz–Radzin tradition treats Shabbos as the moment when a person recognizes that the divine source underlies the work of the entire week, sharpening the symbolism of the Shabbos garden.

paragraphs.text: Shabbat 32a; Proverbs 20:27.  English translation of source: “‘I called you ‘first,’ and I warned you concerning the first [of your dough]. The soul I placed within you is called a ‘lamp,’ and I warned you concerning the lamp. If you observe these commandments, well and good; but if not, I shall take your soul.’ The verse cited for the image is Proverbs 20:27: ‘The soul of man is the lamp of the Lord, searching all the chambers of the belly.’”  Context and connection: The Gemara’s immediate discussion concerns care in three mitzvos and the gravity of neglect. Rav Tzadok reads their deeper structure: niddah repairs ruach and blood, challah relates to the earthly nefesh, and Shabbos light addresses the neshamah. This threefold correspondence is his interpretation, not the Gemara’s explicit enumeration of soul-levels.

Further parallel — Takanat HaShavin 15 [paragraph 205] (English translation as supplied in Akiva Publishing interlinear library):  “And the three letters of Adam correspond to the three soul divisions of Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah deriving from the three worlds of Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah which extend from the World of the Throne downward; their physical dwellings residing in the brain (Mo'ach - Neshamah), heart (Lev - Ruach), and liver (Kaved - Nefesh), as is known.”
Connection to this note: This provides an explicit parallel within Kisvei Rav Tzadok for assigning nefesh, ruach, and neshamah to liver, heart, and brain, respectively.

English translation of the Hebrew: “How is the mitzvah of challah explained? She defiled the challah of the world. She extinguished Adam’s lamp, as it is written, “The soul of a human is God’s lamp”; therefore she must observe the lighting of the lamp.”
Connection to this footnote: This is a close independent Chassidic presentation of the very three-mitzvah Midrash interpreted in Ois 5.

paragraphs.text: Genesis 2:6–7; 1:24.  English translation of source: “Genesis 2:6–7: ‘A mist rose from the earth and watered the whole face of the ground. Then the Lord God formed the human being from dust of the ground, breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the human became a living soul.’ Genesis 1:24: ‘God said: Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds—cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their kinds; and it was so.’”  Context and connection: The Midrash likens the first human’s formation to the making of dough. Rav Tzadok therefore associates challah—separating sanctity from flour and water—with the repair of nefesh, the vital force within embodied life. The analogy goes beyond the literal wording of Bereishis.

Further parallel — Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals, segment 3 [paragraph 1] (English translation as supplied in Akiva Publishing interlinear library):  “The mitzvah of Challah following Terumah: for Terumah is separated from raw grain which is an act of Heaven, the Blessed Name causing it to grow, as in the Midrash (Vayikra Rabbah 28:2) regarding the Omer offering; Terumah being the acknowledgment in all natural creations that all is from Hashem. But Challah is separated from kneaded dough, which is an artifact of human labor, as the Sages noted (Bereishit Rabbah 11:6) contrasting raw wheat with baked cake, human refinement excelling;”
Connection to this note: The earlier passage speaks of Adam as the first dough; this parallel clarifies challah as sanctification within specifically human actions of kneading and preparation.

Connection to this footnote: Challah is explained not only as Adam’s original dough but also as repairing separation by sanctifying a unified whole.

paragraphs.text: Sotah 5a, with Tosafos ad loc..  English translation of source: “Sotah 5a: ‘Rabbi Alexandri said: Anyone who possesses haughtiness—even a light wind stirs him, for it is written, ‘The wicked are like the troubled sea, for it cannot rest.’ And if the sea, which contains so many quarter-measures [of water], is stirred by a slight wind, then a human being, in whose body there is only a quarter-log of blood, all the more so!’ Tosafos, s.v. ‘A person who has only a quarter-log of blood’: ‘Rabbeinu Chananel explains: This is the clear blood upon which the heart is sustained; its weight is only twenty-five sela, which is a quarter of a log.’”  Context and connection: This distinction serves a specific purpose in his argument. The bodily blood of the organs represents nefesh, whereas the refined vitality of the heart corresponds to ruach. Accordingly he connects the niddah-related repair to the place where inner emotional and spiritual life is situated. The precise physiological language belongs to the traditional exegetical model, not modern anatomy.

Further parallel — Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Eruvin, segment 3 [paragraph 14] (English translation as supplied in Akiva Publishing interlinear library):  “For as is known from Bereishit Rabbah (parashah 14), there are five levels to the soul: Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah, Chayah, and Yechidah. Connection to this note: This passage independently locates action in the liver and speech/ruach in the heart. It directly corroborates the distinctions Rav Tzadok makes here between blood, nefesh, and ruach.

Connection to this footnote: This provides a broader Chassidic framework for the distinct levels Rav Tzadok associates with the body, heart, and soul.

paragraphs.text: Beitzah 16a; Exodus 31:17.  English translation of source: “‘Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: The Holy One, blessed be He, gives a person an additional soul on the eve of Shabbos, and at the departure of Shabbos it is taken from him, as it says, ‘He ceased and was refreshed [vayinafash]’ [Exodus 31:17]. Once Shabbos has ceased—woe [vai], the soul [nefesh] is lost!’”  Context and connection: Rav Tzadok treats the additional neshamah as a special Shabbos attainment rather than a weekday possession. His point explains why the lamp, unlike challah and niddah, has a particular weekly role: it signals the return of an encompassing holiness and a foretaste of the World to Come.

Further parallel — Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvot, segment 2 [paragraph 176] (English translation as supplied in Akiva Publishing interlinear library):  “And as we wrote above, at that stage one tastes a foretaste of the World to Come, as recorded at the opening of the second chapter of Beitzah (16a): Shammai would eat every day in honor of the Sabbath, whereas Hillel said: "Blessed be the Lord day by day." The meaning is: the Sabbath is a foretaste of the World to Come, as stated in chapter HaRo'eh (Berakhot 57b); and in the daily psalm recited by the Levites in the Holy Temple: "for the day that is entirely Sabbath and rest for everlasting life"; as written in Berakhot (17a): in the World to Come the righteous sit with crowns on their heads and derive pleasure from the radiance of the Shechinah.”
Connection to this note: The parallel explains the extra Shabbos soul through the experience of the World to Come; it supplements the Gemara about the neshamah yeseirah.

English translation of source: “‘Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for those whose hearts are upright.’”  Context and connection: Rav Tzadok understands the righteous, particularly the person who guards the covenant and resists the yetzer, as fit to receive a higher light. Further parallel — Tzidkat HaTzadik 261 [paragraph 1] (English translation as supplied in Akiva Publishing interlinear library):  “The Holy One, blessed be He, His glory fills the whole earth, and there is no place devoid of Him, only that He is in deep concealment, "He made darkness His secret place" (Psalms 18:12). And when this recognition shines into man's heart—how Hashem fills the whole earth with His glory— this is termed "He brought us forth from darkness to a great light," as recited in the Haggadah.”
Connection to this note: The passage identifies liberation from darkness with the revelation of divine presence, helping explain the specific promise of light granted to the righteous.
Additional Chassidus source — Tiferet Shlomo, on Festivals, Sukkot, source segment 20

paragraphs.text: English translation of the Hebrew: “The hidden light of the six days of Creation was concealed for the righteous in the future—that is, for the righteous of every generation who would come, even in our own day. That illumination is revealed on Shabbosos and festivals.”
Connection to this footnote: The concealed light is described as available to the righteous across the generations and as manifest especially on holy days.

paragraphs.text: Taanit 15a; Psalms 97:11.  English translation of source: “‘Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: I too say that not everyone [is destined] for light, and not everyone for gladness. The righteous are [destined] for light, and the upright for gladness. The righteous for light, as it says, ‘Light is sown for the righteous’; and the upright for gladness, as it says, ‘And for the upright of heart, gladness’ [Psalm 97:11].’”  Context and connection: Rav Tzadok employs this rabbinic pairing to distinguish the revelation of higher light through Written Torah from the illuminating delight of Oral Torah, which straightens understanding and the heart. This identification of the two Torah dimensions is his own interpretive continuation.

Further parallel — Sod Yesharim, Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot, section 2, paragraph 1 (translated directly from the Hebrew archive):  “My father, the holy Gaon of blessed memory, explained that on Shabbos there is every perfection. For from the side of the Blessed Name, there is a great expansion, as the holy Zohar states (Yisro 88a): 'By it all the supernal days are blessed.' And from the side of man there is great contraction; for whoever wishes to have a share and recognition in the spreading of His blessed light that shines on Shabbos must, for his own part, greatly contract himself.”

Connection to this note: This teaching from the Radzin corpus presents Shabbos as both an expansion of divine light and an inward restraint by the human being; the translation here is made afresh from the Hebrew-only archive.
Additional Chassidus source — Bnei Yissaschar, Shabbatot 6, source segment 21.1

English translation of the Hebrew: “The Shabbos lamp is an illumination from the hidden light, of which it is written, “God saw that the light was good.” Therefore the lighting of lamps is described in Scripture by the expression of making good the lamps; some of our earlier masters were meticulous to light thirty-six lamps corresponding to the thirty-six hours during which the hidden light served Adam before it was concealed.”
Connection to this footnote: The statement directly connects the Shabbos lamp to the primordial light reserved for the righteous.

paragraphs.text: Proverbs 13:9.  English translation of source: “‘The light of the righteous rejoices, but the lamp of the wicked is extinguished.’”  Context and connection: Rav Tzadok joins this verse to Tehillim’s ‘Light is sown for the righteous.’ Together they show both a light bestowed from above and a light that grows into joy through the right ordering of the heart. In his reading, this points to the relationship between Written and Oral Torah.

Further parallel — Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Introduction [paragraph 9] (English translation as supplied in Akiva Publishing interlinear library):  “my friend, the eminent and pious Rabbi Eliezer Tzvi Ziegelman, may his lamp shine, remarked: it is named after the verse, "but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings" [Exodus 10:23], since the first treatise in this holy work discusses the exile and Exodus from Egypt, thus far his words. But in my view, it is named after the verse (Psalms 97:11): "Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart." And it is stated in the holy Zohar (I, 45b) and in Zohar Chadash (Bereishit 8c): When the Holy One, blessed be He, gazed upon those generations of the wicked, He concealed the primordial light for the righteous, as it is written: "Light is sown for the righteous, etc."; see there. And in Sefer HaBahir (sec. 147) on this verse: The Holy One, blessed be He, took from His good light and included within it the thirty-two paths of Wisdom, bestowing it upon this world... which is none other than the treasury of the Oral Torah; see there.”
Connection to this note: The title of Ohr Zarua LaTzadik is linked directly to the verse in this note and to the light concealed for the righteous.
Additional Chassidus source — Shem MiShmuel, Re'eh 7, source segment 18

English translation of the Hebrew: “Bar Kappara said in the Midrash: The soul and the Torah were compared to a lamp. The soul, as Scripture says, “The soul of man is the lamp of Hashem”; and the Torah, as it says, “A commandment is a lamp and Torah is light.” The Holy One said to man: My lamp is in your hand—this is Torah; your lamp is in My hand—this is the soul. If you guard My lamp, I shall guard yours.”
Connection to this footnote: The pairing of Torah and soul as two lamps sharpens the contrast between the light of the righteous and the extinguished lamp of the wicked.

paragraphs.text: Genesis 7:11.  English translation of source: “‘In the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month—on that very day all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the windows of heaven were opened.’”  Context and connection: The Zohar makes the year-number a symbolic sign for the sixth millennium: earthly wellsprings and heavenly openings correspond to different manifestations of wisdom. Rav Tzadok’s reading reverses the Flood’s destructive imagery into the possibility of a new release of Torah illumination capable of helping a person return.

Further parallel — Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach, teaching 3 (English translation as supplied in Akiva Publishing interlinear library):  “Behold, this thought of Hashem, blessed be He, became known to Noah inasmuch as profound awe was ingrained in his heart after the Deluge, that it is inappropriate for man to expand himself unchecked according to his own desire, and he must only restrain his spirit; from this he understood that such was likewise the will of Hashem, blessed be He, that He would not curse the ground anymore.”
Connection to this note: The Flood produces lasting reverence and self-restraint; this gives the image of the fountains breaking open a moral counterpoint within Ishbitz thought.
Additional Chassidus source — Shem MiShmuel, Noach 6, source segment 8

English translation of the Hebrew: “In the generation of the Flood there came, in reincarnation, very elevated souls that had fallen among the husks since the days of Adam. The holy Zohar says that destructive angels accompanied the Flood waters; accordingly, it may be said that those souls suffered afflictions at their hands throughout the twelve months, until they were cleansed for a further incarnation.”
Connection to this footnote: This supplies a distinct Chassidic reading of the Flood waters as a process of purification, not only destruction.

paragraphs.text: Genesis 6:9.  English translation of source: “‘These are the generations of Noah: Noah was a righteous man, wholehearted in his generations; Noah walked with God.’”  Context and connection: Rav Tzadok gives ‘righteous’ its further kabbalistic force: the tzaddik is connected with yesod, the covenantal foundation. Because Noach resisted his generation’s corruption, the six-hundredth year of his life becomes an apt symbolic marker for the point called yesod within yesod.

Further parallel — Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach, teaching 7 (English translation as supplied in Akiva Publishing interlinear library):  “and it is brought in the Midrash (Bereishit Rabbah 39:7): the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Abraham our father: You I exempt from honoring a father. The concept in this is that with Noah Hashem likewise sealed a covenant, yet the covenant sealed with Noah was not in the manner He sealed with Abraham our father, peace be upon him; for with Noah Hashem, blessed be He, sealed a covenant according to derekh eretz (natural worldly order) as explained, and as it is stated: 'And I will establish My covenant with you; neither shall all flesh be cut off anymore', since following the awe of the Deluge he accepted upon himself not to expand unchecked as mentioned, and Hashem, blessed be He, likewise agreed not to destroy the world, and Noah began to engage in derekh eretz,”
Connection to this note: Mei HaShiloach distinguishes the natural covenant with Noach from the later covenant with Avraham, sharpening the role of the righteous figure within the Flood narrative.
Additional Chassidus source — Tiferet Shlomo, on Torah, Noach, source segment 1

paragraphs.text: English translation of the Hebrew: “This entire verse hints at the Shabbos day, for the essence of rest is found on Shabbos. Elsewhere the holy Zohar says concerning Shabbos that it is rest above and rest below, and all the blessings above and below depend on the seventh day. Here, too, the Zohar explains that Noach corresponds to the Shabbos day.”
Connection to this footnote: The correspondence between Noach and Shabbos deepens the Torah’s description of him as a righteous person and a source of rest.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I, Vayeira 117a (conclusion as preserved in Pri Tzaddik).  English translation of source: “‘In the six-hundredth year of the sixth [millennium], the gates of wisdom above will open, and the springs of wisdom below, and the world will be readied to enter into the seventh, like a person preparing on the sixth day, once the sun has begun to set, to enter into Shabbos. So too [with the world]. And your sign is: ‘In the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life ... all the fountains of the great deep burst open’ [Genesis 7:11].’”  Context and connection: The sequence of images is essential: opening wisdom is preparation for a sanctified seventh period, not an end in itself. Rav Tzadok interprets the number six hundred through the six middos and the human task of refining desire; the final approach to Shabbos denotes a divine completion beyond human effort. The wording follows the excerpt in Pri Tzaddik because Zohar editions use differing foliation.

paragraphs.text: Further parallel — Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 1, paragraphs 48, 49, 50, 51 (English translation as supplied in Akiva Publishing interlinear library):  “And this is what the Talmud states (Sanhedrin 97a): “Six thousand years the world will exist”; which refers to the temporal garments of this world that will dissolve in the Seventh Millennium, having boundaries in time just as they hold boundaries across the six dimensions of space, whereupon the inward essence and divine depth will radiate eternally. Therefore one illuminated by the Sabbath light, looking solely into the essence within the garments, cleaves to the light that transcends all boundaries.”

Connection to this note: Beis Yaakov explicitly describes the passage from the sixth millennium’s bounded garments into a seventh-millennium revelation; the wording is an independent parallel to Ois 6, not the Zohar text itself.
Additional Chassidus source — Shem MiShmuel, Eikev 5, source segment 9

English translation of the Hebrew: “All the commandments and repairs from the many incarnations are gathered together, and from them a complete, repaired stature is formed. So the world proceeds through the six thousand years of its existence until the seventh millennium, all of which is Shabbos.”

Connection to this footnote: The sixth millennium prepares and gathers the many partial acts of repair into the wholeness of the seventh, complementing Rav Tzadok’s concluding account of the opened gates of wisdom.
